You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test is in the StringUtils.equals() method, which is supposed to compare two CharSequence objects. The test involves comparing a standard String (FOO) with a StringBuilder holding the same characters. The current implementation of StringUtils.equals(CharSequence cs1, CharSequence cs2) first checks for reference equality (cs1 == cs2), then for nulls, and finally calls cs1.equals(cs2).

The provided bug report clarifies a fundamental issue: the JavaDoc for CharSequence explicitly states that equals() is not guaranteed to work consistently across differing implementations of CharSequence. For example, String.equals(StringBuilder) is not guaranteed to return true even if the character sequences are identical because equals is not overridden in StringBuilder to compare contents but is inherited from Object (which checks reference equality). Therefore, the behavior of cs1.equals(cs2) when they are different implementations of CharSequence (like String and StringBuilder) is undefined and should not be relied upon.

The failing test's assertion expects the equals method to compare successful content equality (the characters of String and StringBuilder match), but the current implementation just delegates to cs1.equals(cs2), which compares objects by their own equals definition, not by content.

This design causes inconsistent and unexpected outcomes. The method should explicitly perform content equality comparison (character by character or using a known robust comparison method) rather than rely on cs1.equals(cs2).

No relevant information from the recent bug reports suggests otherwise. The critical insight comes from the current bug report stating the unreliability of equals for CharSequence interfaces with different implementations.

Thus, the root cause is that StringUtils.equals relies on CharSequence.equals, which is undefined behavior when comparing instances of different classes implementing CharSequence, leading to incorrect results in tests like the given one.

Recommended fix: Change StringUtils.equals to perform an explicit content comparison between cs1 and cs2 rather than relying on cs1.equals(cs2). This approach ensures consistent and correct equality checking for all CharSequence implementations.

Next, I can identify any auxiliary methods used by equals, or if the test or related methods provide further insights.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The test failure is related to StringUtils.equals(CharSequence, CharSequence) method in Apache Commons Lang. The current implementation (Lines 781-789) checks for object identity, nulls, and then defers to cs1.equals(cs2). This is problematic because the interface CharSequence does not define a consistent equals() contract for different implementations (e.g., String vs. StringBuilder). The JavaDoc note cited in the bug report confirms this undefined behavior for equals of CharSequence implementations.

Because different CharSequence implementations may not override equals properly (StringBuilder inherits Object.equals(), which only tests reference equality), the method's reliance on cs1.equals(cs2) causes false negatives (content-equal CharSequences of different types appear unequal).

The equalsIgnoreCase method comparison is instructive — it uses CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches(...) for content comparison rather than equals(). This suggests the recommended fix: implement equals(CharSequence, CharSequence) by explicit content comparison, character by character, or using CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches, rather than cs1.equals(cs2).

CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches implements region-based comparison, and when the two CharSequences are not Strings, it falls back to converting to String and comparing regions of those strings, ensuring content equality rather than delegation to equals.

This design aligns with the intended behavior of StringUtils.equals to test for equivalence of character sequences regardless of underlying class type.

Hence, the root cause is that StringUtils.equals currently relies on cs1.equals(cs2), which is undefined for CharSequence objects of different runtime classes, leading to test failures when comparing, for instance, a String with a StringBuilder holding the same characters.

The bug report perfectly matches this analysis indicating StringUtils.equals() doesn't behave correctly for CharSequences due to Java's undefined equals contract for CharSequence. No relevant information in recent bug reports contradicts this.

The fix should be to replace or augment StringUtils.equals(CharSequence, CharSequence) with explicit content comparison logic similar to CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches but exact equality (not ignoring case).

Next steps: Identify the StringUtils.equals() method as the point of fix. Possibly also employ or build upon CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches method for the character-by-character comparison.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
